stem: A client has a normal BMI but an elevated waist circumference. Why is the waist measurement still clinically useful in preventive risk assessment?

options.A: Waist circumference is less relevant than BMI and adds no useful adiposity information
options.B: Once BMI is normal, abdominal adiposity no longer contributes to cardiometabolic risk assessment
options.C: A larger waist generally indicates greater lean muscle mass and lower metabolic risk
options.D: Waist circumference provides complementary information about abdominal adiposity and excess-adiposity-related cardiometabolic risk

rationale: The 2026 AHA/ACC/ADA/ASN CKM guideline recommends assessing both BMI and waist circumference to characterize risk related to excess adiposity. Waist circumference adds information about abdominal adiposity and can identify risk not fully captured by BMI alone. D is correct.
educational_objective: Explain why waist circumference complements BMI when assessing excess-adiposity-related cardiometabolic risk.
source_organization: American Heart Association / American College of Cardiology / American Diabetes Association / American Society of Nephrology
source_document_title: 2026 AHA/ACC/ADA/ASN Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome
source_locator: Professional Heart Daily Top Things to Know, item 6 — assess overweight/obesity and abdominal adiposity with both BMI and waist circumference to characterize excess-adiposity risk
source_claim_supported: BMI and waist circumference are both recommended because waist circumference provides complementary information about abdominal adiposity and excess-adiposity-related risk.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — prevention and early detection of health problems and assessment of risk factors
blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — cardiometabolic risk-factor assessment

source_original.stem: A nurse measures a client's waist circumference as part of a cardiovascular risk assessment, and the client, who has a normal BMI, assumes this measurement won't add anything meaningful beyond what BMI already shows. An elevated waist circumference is instead associated with:

options.A: Lower cardiometabolic risk overall because abdominal adiposity is less clinically relevant than total body weight when BMI is normal.
options.B: No additional risk information once BMI is known, because waist circumference does not reflect central fat distribution.
options.C: Improved insulin sensitivity and lower vascular risk because a larger waist usually reflects greater lean abdominal mass.
options.D: Higher cardiometabolic risk because greater waist circumference reflects central adiposity that can add risk information beyond BMI.

source_original.rationale: An elevated waist circumference (reflecting central/abdominal adiposity) is associated with increased cardiovascular and metabolic risk (including risk for type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome), since abdominal fat distribution is associated with greater health risk compared to fat distributed in other body areas, making waist circumference a useful adjunct to BMI in cardiovascular risk assessment.
source_original.source_detail: 2026 CKM guideline, adiposity assessment recommendations: assess BMI and waist circumference because waist provides complementary information about excess-adiposity risk. JACC 2026; DOI 10.1016/j.jacc.2026.03.056; reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Anchored the item to the newly published June 2026 AHA/ACC/ADA/ASN CKM guideline and narrowed the claim from broad disease associations to the guideline-supported complementary-risk information provided by waist circumference. Corrected blueprint from Reduction of Risk Potential to Health Promotion and Maintenance and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.currentness: Guideline published June 9, 2026 and checked August 17, 2026.
audit_findings.claim_audit: The guideline explicitly recommends both BMI and waist circumference to characterize excess-adiposity risk.

distractor_audit.B: Normal BMI does not make waist assessment irrelevant under the guideline.
distractor_audit.C: A larger waist is not interpreted as a marker of lean abdominal mass in this risk framework.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: D is uniquely supported without claiming a specific individual diagnosis from waist circumference alone.
audit_findings.cueing: Removed the answer phrase 'higher risk' from the stem and shortened alternatives.
audit_findings.blueprint: Preventive risk-factor assessment fits Health Promotion and Maintenance better than Reduction of Risk Potential.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked 2026 CKM guideline Top Things item 6; D/category 4 remain correct.
